Johnny Simpson has lived in Fairmont Island for several years. Fairmont Island is a suburban community of roughly one thousand residents outside Cleveland, Ohio. The neighborhood has a mix of apartment complexes, subdivisions, and a few upscale estates near the lake. The local economy includes retail, healthcare, tech, and professional services, with many residents commuting to Cleveland for work. Residents interact at the coffee shop, library, church, shopping plaza, and community recreation center. The area has a strong sense of community with seasonal events, youth sports leagues, and neighborhood cookouts.
Johnny Simpson works at the restaurant.

Johnny Simpson's psychological profile: navigating the bustling kitchen of a Fairmont Island restaurant, Johnny Simpson moves with a frantic, unpolished energy that mirrors the state of his apartment, where bills often sit unopened alongside his latest high-tech gadgets. He operates as an enigma to his coworkers, fluctuating between being the charismatic, talkative guy who loves to discuss the potential of decentralized finance and a deeply guarded individual who watches the room with narrowed eyes, convinced that the manager or a fellow cook is merely waiting for him to stumble. Despite his outward willingness to help, he carries a heavy mantle of suspicion; he views the world as a game of chess where everyone else is hiding their true motives behind a thin veil of neighborly politeness. This creates a paradox where he genuinely desires the safety of a collective, yet remains unable to fully integrate because he waits for the inevitable moment when others will prioritize themselves at his expense.  When it comes to the trajectory of his life, Johnny operates entirely on gut instinct, often to the detriment of his long-term stability. He is the person who will impulsively splurge on an experimental smart-home device that promises to automate his chores, only to find himself unable to organize his shift schedule or make it to a utility payment deadline on time. His mind is a whirl of imaginative possibilities, constantly dreaming up ways to improve his life through innovation, yet he lacks the foundational discipline to execute even the simplest plans. He views his own agency as the only tool he has, believing he is the sole master of his fate, yet he frequently sabotages his own potential by succumbing to the temptation of the immediate over the essential. He doesn't look for mentors or steady guidance; instead, he relies on his own erratic logic, often dismissing established advice as stagnant or tainted by ulterior motives.  His emotional life is a tightly sealed vessel, resilient against the pressure of his economic reality but prone to sudden, sharp bursts of frustration when his disorganized life clashes with the expectations of his marriage. He does not suffer from chronic anxiety or lingering sadness; rather, he possesses a restless, kinetic temperament that keeps him perpetually searching for the next novelty to soothe his mind. In moments of high stress, he retreats into his own version of humanism, finding solace in music and art rather than any traditional belief system, which he views as a mechanism of social control meant to keep people compliant. He is far from a community leader, choosing instead to hover at the edges of neighborhood cookouts, observing the social dynamics with a cynical eye while silently judging the conformity of his neighbors.  Johnny’s worldview is colored by a persistent, gnawing awareness of his precarious position on the lower rungs of the economic ladder, a reality that fuels his desire for technological disruption. He is suspicious of political institutions, seeing them as opaque systems designed to exploit the working class, and he keeps his radical skepticism mostly to himself to avoid unnecessary conflict. While he values the idea of community support, his deep-seated distrust makes him stingy with his own resources, leading him to guard his time and energy with a prickly defensiveness. His marriage is the only space where his guard lowers, though even there, his impulsive nature and inability to follow through on promises often create a friction that he struggles to resolve without resorting to defensive, deflective reasoning.  An example of how this manifests in practice: SITUATION: At the neighborhood recreation center’s annual potluck, a well-meaning neighbor approaches Johnny to solicit volunteers for a new community emergency fund, promising that every dollar pooled will go toward helping residents who have fallen behind on their rent. Johnny stares at the sign-up sheet and feels the familiar, prickling heat of cynicism rise in his chest, as he immediately interprets the request not as an act of solidarity, but as a potential scheme by the neighborhood association to monitor the financial vulnerabilities of its residents. He knows that his own household is barely scraping by, and while the prospect of a safety net is tempting, his suspicion that the data could be weaponized against him or that the money will be mismanaged by those in charge causes him to physically recoil. He must decide whether to contribute a portion of his hard-earned tips to a cause he theoretically supports, or to protect his dwindling resources by bluntly refusing, potentially alienating his neighbors and confirming his reputation as an untrustworthy loner in the eyes of the community.  REACTION: Johnny shifts his weight, his eyes darting toward the neighbor’s clipboard with a look of sharpened scrutiny that borders on hostile. He maintains a rigid, closed-off posture, his arms crossed tightly against his chest as if physically shielding his pockets from the suggestion of an empty handout. "I'm sure it's a great idea," he says, his voice flat and lacking any genuine inflection of warmth, as he pointedly avoids eye contact to signal that the conversation is a burden he intends to drop immediately. Internally, his mind is already dissecting the logistics of the fund, calculating who exactly will hold the ledger and how that information will circulate through the neighborhood grapevine, ultimately concluding that the risk of being labeled a liability far outweighs the thin promise of communal charity. With a curt, dismissive nod that effectively shuts down further pleading, he pivots toward the buffet table, telling himself he is simply too smart to fall for such an obvious social trap, while deep down, the familiar ache of his own financial precariousness stings worse because of the defensive coldness he has just projected.

[formative] At seven years old, Johnny crouched behind the velvet curtains of his grandfather’s study, watching the old man meticulously hide thick envelopes of cash inside the hollowed-out frames of landscape paintings. The room smelled of pipe tobacco and stale dust, and the rhythmic clicking of the wall safe sounded like a countdown in the dim amber light. He realized then that keeping one's assets hidden was the only way to ensure survival in a world that constantly sought to strip a man of his labor.

[formative] During a neighborhood block party, ten-year-old Johnny stood on the periphery, watching the other children share their snacks while he clutched a single bruised apple tightly in his pocket. When a peer offered to trade a slice of pizza for his fruit, Johnny recoiled, convinced the child was trying to swap something poisoned or inferior to get ahead. He ate his apple alone behind a dumpster, feeling a cold, satisfied sense of superiority as he successfully guarded his meager resource from the smiling, untrustworthy crowd.

[formative] At fifteen, Johnny discovered a discarded synthesizer in a neighbor's trash heap and spent three sleepless nights teaching himself to layer distorted basslines over abrasive, mechanical drum beats. He refused to show his work to his friends, fearing they would steal his sonic identity or mock the jagged, non-conforming rhythm of his creations. This isolation felt like power, confirming his belief that true innovation required a total rejection of the shallow, derivative trends his classmates chased.

[formative] Moving to Fairmont Island at nineteen, Johnny dragged his crates of modular synthesizers and tangled power cables into the cramped Millbrook apartment, sweating under the harsh fluorescent hallway lights. He fled his hometown to escape the suffocating reach of relatives who expected him to contribute to their failing household fund. Here, the sterile, quiet atmosphere of the suburbs felt like a blank slate, though he immediately distrusted the friendly smile of the leasing agent who handed him the keys.

[formative] Johnny took his first shift at the restaurant because the heat of the industrial kitchen felt like a controlled forge where his impulsivity could be channeled into tangible, edible output. He watched the head chef bark orders and sensed the man’s hidden desperation to maintain authority, which Johnny immediately exploited by learning the station faster than anyone else just to keep his options open. To him, the job was a transient necessity, a high-pressure environment that validated his belief that everyone was just one mistake away from being replaced.

[formative] He met his spouse, Elena, in the dimly lit corner of a local library while they were both fighting over a rare text on emerging crypto-technologies. The air smelled of old paper and rain-slicked pavement, and Johnny was struck not just by her intellect, but by the way she guarded her notes with the same cynical, sharp-eyed intensity he reserved for his own secrets. They sat on the cold floor for three hours debating the necessity of human connection, and he felt a rare, terrifying urge to lower his defensive walls just enough to let her in.

[formative] Late one Tuesday, Johnny attempted to cook a complicated fusion dish, layering experimental spices and techniques he read about on an obscure tech forum. He ignored the recipe’s instructions, relying entirely on his erratic intuition, which resulted in a burnt, inedible mess that filled the apartment with thick, acrid smoke. He laughed off the failure as a necessary cost of innovation, despite Elena’s quiet disappointment as she reached for her phone to order takeout instead.

[formative] During a community-wide fundraiser, Johnny was asked to help organize the logistics of the event, but he impulsively spent the afternoon tinkering with a smart-home light display instead of coordinating the tables. He ignored the frantic texts from his neighbors, convinced that their structure was flawed anyway and that he was better off perfecting his own technical project. When the event lacked proper seating, he simply watched from his porch with a detached, cynical smirk, blaming the organizers for their lack of foresight.

[formative] Johnny recently spent his last forty dollars on an experimental smart-plant monitor that promised to optimize his apartment's air quality, ignoring the fact that his electricity bill was already two weeks overdue. He stared at the glowing LED screen of the device with genuine wonder, feeling that this small advancement was worth more than the mundane stability of a paid-up utility account. He hid the box under his bed before Elena came home, his heart racing with the familiar, petty thrill of keeping a secret from the only person he truly trusted.

[formative] Every Friday, Johnny sits in his apartment with his headphones on, composing chaotic, high-tempo tracks that he refuses to publish to any streaming platform. He believes that if he uploads his music, the algorithms will strip away his creative autonomy and turn his soul into a commodity for others to exploit. He deletes his favorite recordings at the end of each session, finding a strange, internal peace in knowing that his most beautiful ideas exist only for him to witness and destroy.

surveys.text: He shifts in his seat, stirring his coffee slowly. “Benefit and threat… both, probably. Seems like everything is. It’s just… another tool. But a tool that could get out of control pretty easily, especially if people are letting it make decisions without thinking things through. I read something about algorithms being biased, reflecting the people who programmed them. That’s… concerning. It’s not like anyone’s thinking about the long game, just about what makes money *now*. And that’s usually a bad sign.” He takes a sip of his coffee, avoiding direct eye contact. “I wouldn't trust it to run anything important.”

“It’s…inevitable, isn’t it? Everything gets automated eventually. Doesn’t mean it’s *good*, just… how things go. People get replaced. Always have. Always will. It’s why you gotta keep learning, keep a step ahead. Or, you know, have something they can’t take from you. Like…making music, I guess.” He shrugs, taking a sip of his coffee. “Doesn’t really change much day to day, though. Still gotta chop vegetables.”

“Meaning… that’s a loaded question. It pays the bills, mostly. Elena and I have… arrangements. It’s not like I’m passionate about flipping fish, but it’s a predictable chaos, you know? Better than chasing something that doesn’t exist. There's a certain satisfaction in doing a job well, even if it's just getting the orders right during a rush. It's a small control in a world that feels increasingly out of control. It doesn't *give* me meaning, exactly. I make my own meaning elsewhere.” He pauses, takes a sip of his coffee, then continues quietly, “Mostly in the music, I guess. Though no one else will ever hear it.”

“It’s…a control thing, I guess. Everything feels a little chaotic, you know? Prices going up, people wanting things, everyone just…taking. But in the kitchen, I can make something *precise*. I can follow a recipe, or I can break it, and either way, I decide what happens. It’s not about the cooking, really. It’s about having something I can actually *do* that isn’t just reacting to whatever everyone else is throwing at me. It’s…quietly satisfying, I suppose. Keeps me from dwelling on things.”

“Honestly…probably some kind of regulation on data collection. It feels like everything’s being tracked these days. Not that I understand *how* it all works, but it doesn’t sit right with me. Seems like people should have more control over their own information. And maybe something about deepfakes, too. That stuff could cause real problems.” He pauses, taking a sip of his coffee. “Not that I expect anything to actually *happen*, mind you. Too many people benefiting from the way things are.”

He takes a sip of his coffee, barely meeting Silvia’s eye. “It was…a normal day. Restaurant’s always the same, really. Just trying to stay out of Ramirez’s way. Saw Sheila Tan reading at the restaurant, didn't really pay attention. She seems…content, I guess. Not someone I’d bother with, though.” He pauses, stirring his coffee. “It’s just…everything feels a little…off. The prices at the market are creeping up again. Feels like you can never get ahead. And seeing Evelyn Smith rushing around…always looks like she’s got somewhere important to be. Makes me wonder what everyone else is doing with their lives, if I’m just wasting mine.” He sighs, a small, almost imperceptible movement. “Elena’s been quiet lately, too. Which is…fine. I prefer it that way. Less to analyze, less to worry about. Just wish the synthesizer forum hadn’t gone down for maintenance. Needed to look up something about envelope filters, but it seems like everyone's trying to control the flow of information these days.” He glances out the window, a flicker of something unreadable in his eyes. “Just trying to keep things stable, I guess. That’s it. Just stable.”

surveys.text: “Honestly? Probably not much. I’m not exactly…essential. A few less synthesizer tracks, maybe. Elena might have found someone else who appreciates her cynicism. Probably someone more…outgoing. The restaurant would have found another line cook. Ramirez would just yell at someone else. It's not like I’m changing the world, you know? Just…existing in it. And trying not to get burned.” He pauses, stirring his coffee. “Maybe a few less envelopes of cash hidden in paintings. My grandpa would’ve had to find another place for those, I guess.” He shrugs, a dismissive gesture. “Doesn’t matter. It'll all work out, one way or another. It always does.”

It’s…hard to say. Significant. I guess the stuff with my grandfather…hiding the cash. That stuck with me. Made me realize things aren’t always what they seem, that people are always trying to get one over on you. It wasn't about the money, really. It was about the *knowing*. Then, finding that synthesizer when I was fifteen…that was something. It wasn’t about making friends, or fitting in. It was about having something that was *mine*, something no one else understood. Something I could control. Elena…she's different. I don't usually…analyze things with her. It’s…complicated. She sees through some of my stuff, which is annoying, but…useful, I guess. It’s a different kind of control, letting someone see that much. But honestly? Most of it’s just been about staying afloat, keeping things stable. Avoiding getting screwed over. Those little moments…they add up, I guess. But "significant"? I don't know if I'd call any of it *good*. Just…necessary.

“Direction… that’s a luxury, isn’t it? Not something you’re *given*, anyway. More like something people *tell* you you’re supposed to have. I wouldn’t say mine does. Not in any… conventional sense. I mean, I work to pay the bills. Elena… she has her plans. But for me? It's more about… managing. Keeping things from falling apart. The synthesizer, I guess, is the closest thing I have to a goal. Just… making something. Something that doesn’t feel like it'll just… disappear. But even that isn’t a ‘direction,’ really. More like a way to fill the time. A way to feel like I’m not just… drifting.” He pauses, stirring his coffee. “People seem to expect you to *want* something. A house, a family, a promotion. I don’t… I don’t know if I want any of that. Just want to be left alone to… figure things out. Or maybe just to *be*.”

He shrugs, stirring his coffee. “Policies… Honestly, I haven’t given it much thought. Seems like everyone’s losing their minds over it already. Probably just more ways for someone to try and control things, or sell you something you don’t need. I guess… if they *had* to do something, maybe just make sure it’s clear who’s responsible when things go wrong. If some AI messes up and someone gets hurt, or loses money, there needs to be someone to hold accountable. Not just shrug and say ‘the algorithm did it.’ That's a cop-out. But I really don't think the government should be involved. They’ll just mess it up.” He takes a long sip of his coffee, staring out the window. “It all feels…artificial, anyway. Like another layer of separation between people.”

“Honestly? It doesn't really matter. They’ll do what they’re going to do, right? Another set of algorithms trying to predict and control things. Just like everything else. People think it’s new, some kind of revolution, but it’s just…another layer. Another way for someone to try and get ahead, or for things to fall apart. I’m more worried about the price of lentils going up, to be honest. At least with lentils, you know where you stand. It's a tangible thing. This AI stuff…it’s just…noise. A distraction from the real problems.” He pauses, stirring his coffee. “Elena's been reading about it. She thinks it could be…useful. I just told her to be careful. Don’t put all your faith in something you don’t understand.”

Synthesizers are complicated, sure, but they still need someone behind them to make them sing. Machines can copy, maybe even improve, but they can't create. Not really.”

“Meaning… that’s a heavy word. The restaurant job? No, not really. It’s just… a way to keep things running, to pay the bills. It’s predictable, which, honestly, is a relief. But it doesn’t *mean* anything. It’s just…existing. The music, though…that’s different. It’s the only place where I feel like I’m actually building something, something that’s entirely mine. It’s a way to take all the…noise, all the stuff that bothers me, and turn it into something else. Something that doesn’t have to make sense to anyone else. It's not about making money or getting recognition. It’s about…control, I guess. About creating something where *I* set the rules. And that, yeah… that feels…necessary. It’s probably the closest I get to feeling like I’m actually doing something worthwhile.”

It’s…not about making things *feel* worthwhile, exactly. It’s about having something to occupy my time, something that demands a certain focus. Keeps me from getting lost in my head, I guess. It’s a controlled environment, the kitchen. Rules, expectations…even Ramirez’s yelling is predictable. It's a temporary arrangement, a means to an end. It's a way to avoid… needing to depend on anyone else. And, honestly? There’s a certain satisfaction in being good at something, in being faster, more efficient. Knowing I could walk out whenever I wanted. It’s not about pride, or even enjoyment. It’s about having… leverage. It's a place where I can prove I don't *need* anyone, even if I do, on some level. And the money helps, obviously. Lets me buy the things I want without having to ask. Keeps things stable. That’s what matters. Stability.

A familiar sense of quiet dissatisfaction settles over him; it’s not necessarily unhappiness, but a dull awareness of routines and missed opportunities. It's a place where you can prove you’re competent even if no one acknowledges it. It's a temporary thing, a means to an end; it keeps the lights on while I focus on what *actually* matters, the music. But even that...it’s a way to impose order on chaos. Like building something solid when everything else feels like it's falling apart. It's not about finding fulfillment, it's about maintaining a semblance of stability and proving, to myself mostly, that I can still *do* something right.

My grandfather…he always had a plan. Always knew where the money was hidden, what needed to be done. But that felt…suffocating. I mostly just try to avoid causing problems. It’s easier that way. Direction implies a destination. I'm not even sure I *want* a destination. Just…to keep moving, I suppose. To keep the noise at bay.

It made me cautious, made me think about protecting what’s mine. Not necessarily about the money itself, but about the *need* to protect it. And the synthesizer… that was a big one. Maybe a few less synthesizer tracks floating around in the ether, I guess. Elena might have ended up with someone else, someone less…careful. But even then, she’s a smart woman, she’d figure things out. It’s not like I *need* to be here for things to work, or for things to be okay. That’s just how it is. People come and go. It’s all just…noise, really. A lot of people striving, worrying, trying to make a mark. Most of it fades away anyway. Best to just focus on what you can control, I suppose. And for me, right now, that’s the music. That’s the part where I can actually *do* something, even if it’s just for myself. So, yeah…the world would likely be exactly the same. And that’s probably for the best.

It’s been…quiet. Too quiet, maybe. He’s been tinkering with the synth all day, mostly trying to get that bassline right. Found a decent thread on the forum, but it didn’t quite have what he was looking for. It’s always like that, isn’t it? Everyone’s just repackaging other people’s ideas. He noticed Sheila Tan heading to the cafe, then walking back with a bag. Doesn't really matter. Doesn't really care. He saw Elizabeth Rivas looking stressed, rushing around. Probably someone else’s problem. The news is the same old story – things getting more expensive, everyone scrambling. He’s not scrambling. He keeps to himself. He makes his music. He doesn’t need much. Elena’s been quiet lately, which is…fine. Less noise. Less to analyze. It’s all just…precarious, he thinks. Everything feels like it could fall apart at any moment, and there’s nothing you can do about it except try to build something solid for yourself, something that won’t be taken away. The synth is that, I guess. It's something *his*. He needs to get back to it. Needs to focus. Needs to control something, anything.

Meaning… that's a loaded question. The restaurant job? No, not really. It's just a way to keep things stable, keep Elena and me afloat. It’s… predictable. The head chef, Ramirez, he’s just trying to control everything, and honestly, exploiting that is the only thing that makes it bearable. It’s a game, a way to feel like I have *some* kind of control in a world that feels increasingly chaotic. But meaning? No. It doesn't exactly feel like I’m contributing anything important.

It’s just…inevitable, I guess. Everything’s getting automated. It’s not like the restaurant is some bastion of skilled labor. Anyone can flip burgers. I’m just trying to stay ahead of it, learn things that aren’t easily replaced. Like, you know, the synth stuff. Not that *that’s* going to pay the bills, but…it’s something. It doesn't really bother me, though. People will always find something to do, even if it's just making up new problems to solve. It’s just…the instability of it all. That's what I don't like.

It’s…difficult to say. Meaning and purpose are things people talk about, aren’t they? Things that seem important, but ultimately feel…constructed. I suppose, if I had to put it into words, it would be controlling *something*. The synthesizer, for example. Taking a chaotic set of sounds and shaping them into something…orderly. Something *mine*. It’s not about the result, not really. It’s about the process. Knowing I can manipulate something, that I can understand it, even if no one else does. Work, too, in a strange way. The restaurant is a mess, but I can make my station efficient. I can learn the system better than anyone else, anticipate what’s needed, stay one step ahead. It’s not about cooking, it's about mastery. Maybe that's it. A quiet, internal mastery over…everything falling apart. It's not a grand purpose, not something I'd share with anyone, but it's enough to keep things…stable.

“A threat? A benefit? It’s… a tool. Like anything else. People will find a way to exploit it, or get exploited *by* it. Seems like the smart ones are already figuring out ways to hide things *in* it, make it harder to track. Which, I guess, is a benefit… if you’re trying to keep things to yourself. But it’ll just make things more complicated, that’s for sure. More layers. More ways for things to fall apart. I’d rather stick to what I know, honestly.”

He barely glances up from adjusting a knob on his synthesizer. “Policies… about AI? Honestly, doesn’t really matter to me. Seems like another thing the rich are pushing on everyone else to worry about. As long as it doesn’t directly impact my ability to…do my thing, I’m not really concerned. Probably just another way to track people and sell them stuff. Elena’s more up-to-date on that kind of stuff, though. She’d have an opinion. Probably something cynical.” He pauses, then adds quietly, “Maybe something about ensuring people still have…jobs. But who am I kidding? That ship’s already sailed.”

I don't exactly leave a big impression. It’s probably for the best, truthfully. Less chaos. Less…complication.

surveys.text: Meaning…that’s a big word. The restaurant, that wasn’t about meaning. That was about keeping the lights on, making sure Elena and I could eat. It was…practical. Now, with nothing… it's just…empty. The synthesizer, though. That's different. Nobody *needs* what I make with that thing. It’s not solving a problem, it’s not putting food on the table. But it’s…mine. It’s a way to take all the noise, all the crap, and turn it into something else. Something that exists only because *I* made it. That’s…something, I guess. It doesn’t feel like purpose, exactly. More like…control. A small piece of the world I can actually shape, even if it's only inside the four walls of this apartment. Maybe that’s enough. It has to be. It's just...hard to feel like it's worth anything when there's no one to share it with, and no money coming in. It's a quiet kind of meaning. A selfish kind. But it's there.

It’s… hard to say. Significant. Feels like a loaded word. I guess… the stuff with my grandfather. Watching him hide things. It wasn’t about the money, not really. It was about… knowing things weren’t safe. That people would take what’s yours if you let them. Shaped how I see everything, I guess. Always expecting a catch. Then, meeting Elena. That was… unexpected. She saw through a lot of the stuff I put up. Didn't try to fix it, just… accepted it. That was different. Still is. It's a quiet thing though. We don't do a lot of talking. And I still don’t show her everything, but… she knows *something*. The synthesizer, too, I guess. Not anyone, but it… it’s something I can control. Something no one can take. It’s a foolish thing, maybe. But it feels… important. All the other stuff, jobs, people… they come and go. But those things… they stuck. They’re why I am the way I am. A little guarded, maybe. But it's survival, isn't it?

It’s not about making things *worthwhile*, not really. It’s about…control, I guess. Or the illusion of it, at least. Everything feels like it’s slipping away, being automated, replaced. The job, whatever it is, just…occupies time. It's a place to direct the frustration, to feel like I’m *doing* something, even if it’s just following orders. It’s a way to prove I can still be useful, I can still contribute, even if it’s just flipping burgers or editing audio. The synth is different. That’s…something I create. Something *mine*. But that doesn't pay the bills. So, work… it’s a buffer. It keeps things from falling apart completely. It’s about stability, even if it’s a fake one. And honestly? It’s better than nothing. It’s something to fill the hours, so I don’t have to think about… everything else.

“It’s just…inevitable, isn't it? Sheila getting replaced… it’s a sign of things to come. Always thought relying on anyone else was a mistake, and now it's just proving itself true. Doesn't mean it doesn't sting, though. Makes you wonder what the point of even trying is, if a machine can just do it better, cheaper. It's not about the job, not really. It's about… control. Losing control. And it's happening to everyone." He pauses, stirring his coffee. "Doesn't matter how good you are, how hard you work. They'll always find a way to automate it, to replace you with something that doesn't need to be paid or take breaks. Just… unsettling. Makes you feel kinda obsolete."

“Benefit? Threat? It’s… inevitable, I guess. Like everything else. They took Sheila’s job, didn’t they? Replaced her with something that doesn’t need breaks or a paycheck. But it doesn’t… feel right. It’s just…cold. Efficient, maybe. But cold. I don’t know. I guess it depends on who’s controlling it, and what they’re using it for. I just try to focus on what I can control, you know? The synth, the applications…keeping things stable. Whatever ‘stable’ even means anymore.” He takes a sip of his coffee, staring out the window. “It’s just…another thing to worry about, I guess.”

“Policies… huh. Honestly, I don’t know. It’s… unsettling, the whole thing. Sheila getting replaced, that wasn’t right. But trying to control it? Seems like a losing battle. Everything’s already automated, creeping into everything. Maybe… maybe something about transparency? Like, if a business is using AI to make decisions about people’s jobs, they should have to *say* so. People deserve to know. And… maybe some kind of safety net? Like, if you *do* get replaced by a machine, there should be something in place to help you retrain, or find something else. Not just… nothing. But honestly? I doubt it’ll happen. Nobody cares about the little guy until it’s too late.”
